6. Fill in **Selection Notes** as you read.
7. Take **Selection Check**.
8. Lock it in with **Remember the Four Conditions**.
9. Read **Questions People Ask About Evolution**.
10. Finish with **Investigation: Track the Trait**.

## Nothing Is Trying

Here is a sentence you have probably heard: animals adapt to their environment. It sounds right. It is also the most common way of getting natural selection exactly backwards.

An individual does not adapt. **Populations** change across generations, and no individual in them changes at all.

### Four conditions, and that is the whole thing

Natural selection follows from four facts. If all four hold, it happens. There is nothing else to it.

**One: variation exists.** In any population, individuals differ. Some beetles are darker, some lighter. Some bacteria happen to carry a gene that a particular drug cannot disable. Crucially, **this variation is already there before the environment changes.** It was not requested and it was not produced on demand.

**Two: some of that variation is heritable.** Traits carried in genes get passed to offspring. Traits you acquire during your life do not. A weightlifter's children are not born strong, and a mouse that loses its tail has ordinary tailed pups.

**Three: more offspring are produced than can survive.** Food, space and safety run out. Not everyone makes it.

**Four: survival is not random with respect to those traits.** Some variants do better in this particular environment, so they leave more offspring.

Run those four for many generations and the **frequency** of a trait in the population shifts. That shift is the whole phenomenon.

### Why the wrong version is so appealing

The wrong version says an organism notices a problem and develops a solution. It is appealing because it is how *we* solve problems, and because the results genuinely look designed.

But nothing is trying. A **mutation** does not arrive because it would be useful. Mutations happen regardless, and most are neutral or harmful. Occasionally one turns out to help in the environment that happens to exist, and that one spreads — not because it was needed, but because its carriers left more offspring.

Bacteria make this concrete. Give a large population of bacteria an antibiotic and a few usually survive. Those few were not toughened by the drug. They already carried a variant that the drug could not disable, before it was ever applied. The antibiotic did not create resistance; it removed everything else. The next generation descends from the survivors, so more of it is resistant. Do that repeatedly and resistance becomes common.

This is also why antibiotics are worth using carefully rather than routinely, and why resistance is a serious medical problem rather than a textbook curiosity.

### Fit to what, exactly

**Fitness** in biology does not mean strong or fast. It means leaving more surviving offspring in this environment. A trait that helps in one place can be useless in another and harmful in a third.

So selection has no direction and no destination. Change the environment and the favoured trait can reverse within a few generations. Nothing is being perfected, because there is nothing to be perfect for.

What is left is simpler and stranger than the story people tell. Variation that already existed, filtered by conditions that happen to prevail, repeated until the population looks built for a world that merely selected it.

## How Populations Change

Beetles in one habitat can have different colors. Suppose these differences are inherited and affect how many offspring they leave. Over many **generations**, the share of each color in the **population** can change. This can be evolution by natural **selection**.

Individuals can grow, learn and adjust during life. These **acquired** changes do not, by themselves, show that a population has evolved. We need to track inherited differences across generations.

### Follow the process

**Variation** means that individuals differ. A useful variant may already be present when conditions change. New variants can also arise later through mutation or arrive with new members. Need does not direct a useful **mutation**, which is a change in DNA.

A **heritable** trait can pass from parent to offspring through genes. Many traits also depend on the surroundings. Building muscles through training does not automatically copy those muscles into a child's DNA.

The **environment** affects which traits help. Food, predators and mates all matter. Crowding is not required for selection. A trait might change success in finding a mate or the number of offspring produced.

**Fitness** means success in passing genes to later generations, compared with others in that setting. Survival matters when it affects reproduction. Fitness does not mean strength, health or personal worth.

A helpful inherited trait can become more common. Its **frequency** is how common it is. But this is not guaranteed. Chance can remove even a helpful variant. Changes due to chance are called genetic drift. Drift can occur in any population and often has stronger effects in small ones.

### Read the pictures as models

Our rows of eight beetles have two, then four, then six dark beetles. These are invented counts. They show new generations, not the same beetles changing color. A moth picture shows how a background can affect visibility. It cannot prove selection by itself. We also need evidence about inheritance and offspring.

The bacteria panel is a simple counter model. Assume two bacteria already have inherited **resistance** to one antibiotic. They survive exposure and reproduce. Their descendants can make resistance more common. In real cases, new mutations and genes passed between microbes can also matter. A survivor alone is not proof of resistance. We use counters, not live bacteria or drugs.

### No planned goal

A mutation can be harmful, helpful or have little effect in a given setting. A population may never gain a trait it needs. Natural selection has no plan for a perfect organism.

An **adaptation** is an inherited trait shaped by past selection. It may help in one setting and be a drawback in another. Ask what varied, what was inherited, and how success in reproduction differed. Then consider chance and other possible causes.

from: Darker and lighter moths were both already present in the population. Against sooty trees the darker ones were harder for predators to see, so they survived and reproduced more often. Over generations the proportion of dark moths in the population increased. No moth changed colour, and none of it happened so that anything could hide.
to: In this model, dark and pale variants have a heritable basis. Darker moths may be less visible on dark bark and leave more offspring. Their frequency can then rise across generations. This requires evidence of inheritance and reproductive differences; a picture alone is insufficient. It does not mean individuals changed color because they needed camouflage.

from: Need does not produce variation. Mutations happen regardless of whether they would be useful, and most are neutral or harmful. A trait spreads only if it happens to already exist and happens to help its carriers leave more offspring in the environment that happens to prevail. The usefulness follows from the spread rather than causing it.
to: Need does not direct mutation toward a requested solution. New variants may arise or arrive, and heritable variants that increase reproductive success can be favored by selection. That reproductive advantage can help cause their spread; chance also matters, and even useful variants are not guaranteed to spread.

from: If most mutations are harmful, how does anything ever improve? 🧬
to: Do helpful mutations always spread?

from: Because harmful ones are removed and the rare helpful one spreads. Populations are large and generations are many, so even a very uncommon helpful variant gets its chance. The filter does the work, not the mutation rate.
to: No. A trait may help in one setting but not another. Chance can remove a helpful variant before it spreads.

from: Does natural selection explain everything about how species change?
to: Does selection explain every evolutionary change?

from: No, and biologists are clear about that. Random genetic drift changes small populations by chance alone, and some traits are carried along simply because they sit near a useful gene. Selection is the main mechanism behind traits that look well-suited, not the only thing happening.
to: No. Mutation, arriving or leaving genes, and chance also cause change. Genetic drift is change through chance. Its effects are often stronger in small groups.

from: Are humans still evolving? 🌍
to: Are humans still evolving?

from: Yes. Lactose tolerance in adults spread in populations with a long history of dairy farming, and it is a well-studied recent example. Evolution does not stop; it just happens on a timescale longer than a lifetime.
to: Yes. For example, some human populations have inherited traits that let adults keep digesting milk sugar. Evolution concerns inherited changes across generations, and its pace varies.

from: Is the phrase survival of the fittest wrong? 🤔
to: What can survival of the fittest leave out?

from: It is not wrong so much as badly worded for modern ears. Fittest meant best-fitting to the conditions, not strongest. Because the everyday meaning of fit has drifted, most biologists avoid the phrase entirely.
to: It leaves out reproduction. Fitness concerns the genes passed to later generations compared with others in that setting. It is not a measure of strength or human worth.

from: Why do some organisms look so perfectly designed? 🐦
to: Does adaptation mean perfect design?

from: Because you are seeing the survivors of an enormous filter, and not the countless variants that failed. Looked at closely, organisms are full of awkward compromises, which is what you would expect from something assembled by filtering rather than planning.
to: No. Selection acts on traits that are available. A trait may have costs as well as benefits. A once-useful trait can become less helpful when conditions change.

from: Can a trait become common without being useful at all?
to: Can a neutral variant become common?

from: It can. In a small population, chance alone can make a neutral trait common, which is genetic drift. Usefulness makes spreading much more likely, but it is not the only route.
to: Yes. Chance can make a variant more common even if it does not help reproduction. This is genetic drift.

from: Why does antibiotic resistance matter so much? 💊
to: How does antibiotic resistance fit this lesson?

from: Because we are running the experiment constantly and at scale. Every use of an antibiotic removes susceptible bacteria and leaves resistant ones to reproduce. That is why doctors avoid prescribing them when they will not help, and why you should follow the instructions you were actually given rather than a rule of thumb you half remember.
to: Inherited resistance can help microbes leave offspring when a drug is present. New mutations and genes passed between microbes also matter. One survivor does not prove resistance; real cases need more evidence.

from: The frequency shift is the whole phenomenon and students almost never see one happen. Running it by hand makes the population the thing that changes, and the language audit at the end is where most students discover they have written the wrong version without noticing.
to: Counter generations connect inherited variants, reproductive outcomes and measured frequencies. Model limitations prevent a simple color model from being mistaken for complete biology.

from: You will have a bag of counters in two colours standing for two variants of one heritable trait, plus a rule your teacher gives you for which colour survives in this environment. You may change the environment rule partway through if you say when you did it.
to: Use 40 counters or digital tokens in two colors, initially 20 of each. Color represents a heritable variant in a simplified asexual population. The teacher supplies a survival rule that favors one color without deliberately selecting individual counters. After survivors are counted, make 40 offspring by repeatedly sampling one survivor at random with replacement and adding an offspring of that color to a new group. The new group replaces the parents. State that real inheritance can be more complex. No microbes or antibiotics are used.

to: Use counters only. Do not imply that need directs useful mutations or that organisms never grow or learn.

from: Their first write-up said the population adapted to the new conditions. Running the language audit, they underlined adapted and found it was doing the work of a whole explanation. They rewrote it as a statement about which counters were removed each round and what that did to the proportions, and the sentence got longer and much better.
to: They explained both the survival rule and how they sampled offspring to make the next generation. They reported counts, proportions and any rounds against the trend, and compared the results with a repeat run.

from: The banned words are not a style rule. Each of them hides the mechanism, and being forced around them makes a student state the mechanism out loud.
to: Naming the mechanism and reporting variation across runs is more informative than using or banning a single word such as adapted.

from: Is there a sentence where a single organism changes? Rewrite it.

from: Did any counter change colour at any point? What does that tell you?

from: Six generations, a graph, and an explanation with no organism trying anything.
to: Record six generations with counts and proportions. Include offspring formation, uncertainty and one limitation of the model.

from: An individual does not adapt. Populations change across generations, and no individual in them changes at all.
to: Heritable variants can differ in reproductive contribution. Follow frequencies across generations and distinguish this from growth, learning or acclimation.
